planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Surefire is self-fertile and needs no pollinizer, and is best adapted to zones 4-8.

directions: Surefire is a University of Minnesota tart cherry release prized for blooming roughly one to two weeks later than Montmorency, a trait that lets its flowers dodge the late spring frosts that frequently thin or wipe out crops on earlier-flowering sour cherries. Unlike Montmorency's yellow flesh and clear juice, Surefire's fruit has red flesh and red juice all the way through, giving pies and preserves a deeper color. The tree is self-fertile and needs no second cherry for pollination, and it carries the cold hardiness typical of University of Minnesota fruit introductions. Ripening in mid-summer, it is grown primarily for baking, juice, and preserves rather than fresh eating, like other tart cherries.

common_name: Schattenmorelle Cherry (Rheinische Schattenmorelle, German Heirloom Sour Cherry)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Schattenmorelle is self-fertile and needs no pollinizer, and is best adapted to zones 4-8.

directions: Schattenmorelle, literally 'shadow morello' in German, is a centuries-old Central European heirloom sour cherry long trained as a fan or espalier against cooler, partly shaded walls where sweeter cherries would struggle to ripen well. The nearly black, glossy fruit ripens late in the sour cherry season and is intensely tart with dark, richly colored juice, making it a favorite for kirsch, jam, and strudel fillings across Germany and Central Europe. The tree is self-fertile, and its late bloom gives it some natural protection from the early spring frosts that can damage earlier-flowering cherries. Prune lightly after harvest to renew fruiting wood, since like other sour cherries it fruits on both spurs and the previous year's growth.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Oblačinska is self-fertile, tolerates poor soils, and is best adapted to zones 4-8.

directions: Oblačinska is the sour cherry population at the heart of Serbia's cherry industry, a naturally variable landrace-type selection first identified growing semi-wild near the village of Oblačina and now the backbone of the country's cherry juice, jam, and fruit-brandy production. The small, dark red to nearly black fruit forms in dense clusters on a vigorous, suckering, shrubby tree that tolerates poor soils and harsh continental winters better than many Western named cultivars. Its intense acidity and deep color suit it to processing and preserving far more than fresh eating. Because it suckers freely from the root, it is usually grown in orchard blocks rather than as a single specimen, with root suckers thinned periodically to control spread.
sources: University of Novi Sad Faculty of Agriculture

common_name: Stevnsbær Cherry (Danish Cherry Wine Sour Cherry)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Stevnsbær is self-fertile and winter-hardy enough for Scandinavian climates, and is best adapted to zones 4-8.

directions: Stevnsbær takes its name from the Stevns peninsula on the Danish island of Zealand, where orchards of this small, deep-red sour cherry have long supplied the region's traditional cherry wine and liqueur making. The fruit is highly acidic and intensely flavored, valued far more for cooking, preserving, and fermenting than for fresh eating. The tree is self-fertile and hardy enough to handle cold Scandinavian winters, flowering in spring with the same five-petaled white blossoms typical of sour cherries. Harvest once fruit has turned fully dark red to nearly black for the most concentrated flavor and color in juice or wine.

planting.note: Transplant in spring for best establishment, since sugar maples resent fall root disturbance in colder zones.

directions: Autumn Fest was selected by J. Frank Schmidt & Son Co. for its strong upright growth and dependable central leader, giving it a more uniformly upright-oval form than seedling-grown sugar maples. It grows noticeably faster than typical sugar maple seedlings while holding dark green summer foliage that turns an early, consistent orange-red to red in fall. The vigorous, structurally sound form makes it a dependable choice for street tree and urban plantings where uniformity matters. Like other sugar maples, it performs best in deep, well-drained soil and resents heavy soil compaction and road salt exposure.
sources: J. Frank Schmidt & Son Co. nursery catalog

planting.note: Transplant in spring for best establishment; Autumn Splendor's southern provenance gives it better heat and drought tolerance than typical northern-sourced sugar maple stock.

directions: Autumn Splendor was selected from an isolated population of sugar maple found in Caddo County, Oklahoma, far south and west of the species' usual range, by Dr. John Pair of Kansas State University, and it carries that provenance's unusual heat and drought tolerance. It resists the leaf scorch and premature leaf tatter that afflict typical northern-sourced sugar maples when planted in hot, dry climates, making it a dependable choice for the southern Great Plains. Glossy green summer foliage turns a bright orange-red in fall, giving the classic sugar maple color display on a tree that can actually thrive where standard stock struggles. Give it full sun and well-drained soil, and expect a broadly oval to rounded crown at maturity.
sources: J. Frank Schmidt & Son Co. nursery catalog
Kansas State University John C. Pair Horticultural Center

planting.note: Transplant in spring for best establishment; Flashfire is a Caddo-strain selection bred for heat tolerance in regions too warm for standard sugar maple.

directions: Flashfire was selected from Caddo Mountain sugar maple seedlings for fall color that outshines other heat-adapted selections in its lineage, turning a notably bright, early red rather than the more muted orange-red typical of southern-provenance sugar maples. It shows better mildew resistance than many related Caddo-strain selections while keeping their core advantage: real tolerance for the summer heat that damages northern-sourced sugar maples planted too far south. The broadly oval crown and dark green summer foliage are standard sugar maple traits, but the combination of heat tolerance and standout fall color is what distinguishes this introduction. Plant in full sun with deep, well-drained soil for the strongest color and growth.
sources: J. Frank Schmidt & Son Co. nursery catalog

planting.note: Transplant in spring for best establishment, since sugar maples resent fall root disturbance in colder zones.

directions: Crescendo is a Morton Arboretum selection drawn from the western range of sugar maple, chosen for holding up better to heat and environmental stress than typical eastern-provenance nursery stock. It forms a broadly oval crown with dark green summer foliage that turns orange-red to bright red in fall, and its toughness makes it a practical option for municipal and campus plantings outside the species' usual comfort zone. As with other sugar maples, deep, well-drained soil and protection from de-icing salt will keep it performing at its best over the long term. Expect a sturdy, reliably structured shade tree rather than a novelty form.
sources: J. Frank Schmidt & Son Co. nursery catalog

planting.note: Transplant in spring for best establishment; John Pair is a smaller-stature, heat- and drought-tolerant sugar maple selection suited to the southern plains.

directions: John Pair was selected from a Caddo County, Oklahoma seed source and is named for Dr. John Pair of Kansas State University, who identified it as an outstanding performer under the heat, drought, and drying winds typical of the southern plains. It stays smaller than most sugar maple cultivars, maturing into a symmetrical, rounded tree around 30 feet tall and wide, which makes it easier to fit into smaller residential sites than full-size sugar maple selections. Glossy green summer foliage turns red in fall, bringing the fall color gardeners expect from sugar maple to regions where the straight species often struggles. Site it in full sun with deep, well-drained soil for best performance.
sources: J. Frank Schmidt & Son Co. nursery catalog
Kansas State University John C. Pair Horticultural Center

planting.note: Transplant in spring for best establishment, since sugar maples resent fall root disturbance in colder zones.

directions: Oregon Trail was selected from sugar maples growing in and around Hiawatha, Kansas, a town long known locally as 'the City of Beautiful Maples' for its old planted avenues of the species, with this particular tree traced to stock along the historic Oregon Trail corridor. It forms a broadly oval to rounded crown with dark green summer foliage and strong branch structure, turning orange-red to red in fall. Its prairie-tested resilience makes it a solid choice for Great Plains and Midwest plantings where wind tolerance and structural strength matter as much as fall color. Give it full sun and deep, well-drained soil for the best growth and color.
sources: J. Frank Schmidt & Son Co. nursery catalog
